concepts.title: Slope of a Line Through Two Points
concepts.definition: The slope measures the tilt of a line: it is the rise divided by the run when moving between any two of its points, and it stays the same no matter which pair of points on that line you pick. A horizontal line has slope 0; as the line steepens toward vertical the slope grows without bound and is left undefined at exactly vertical.
concepts.key_idea: One pair of points fixes the tilt for the whole line -- the quotient of rises over runs is constant along a straight line.

concepts.title: Parallel and Perpendicular Conditions
concepts.definition: Two non-vertical lines run parallel exactly when their slopes match, and they meet at a right angle exactly when the product of their slopes is -1; each condition lets you turn a geometric statement about lines into a quick algebraic check.
concepts.formula: m1 = m2 for parallel, m1 * m2 = -1 for perpendicular
concepts.key_idea: Parallel means equal slopes; perpendicular means slopes are negative reciprocals of each other.

concepts.title: Angle Between Two Lines
concepts.definition: When two lines with slopes m1 and m2 cross, each of the two angles between them has a tangent given by the difference of slopes over one plus their product; the denominator hitting zero signals a perfect right angle.
concepts.key_idea: The two crossing angles are supplementary, and one tangent formula with a sign flip covers both choices.

concepts.title: Collinearity of Three Points via Slopes
concepts.definition: Three points lie on one single straight line precisely when the slope joining two of them equals the slope joining a different pair; a mismatch of slopes proves the points form a triangle instead.
concepts.key_idea: Collinearity is a slope comparison: if A, B, C are on one line then slope AB = slope BC.

concepts.title: Point-Slope, Two-Point and Slope-Intercept Forms
concepts.definition: A line is pinned down by a tilt plus one anchor: knowing slope m and a point (x1, y1) gives y - y1 = m (x - x1), while two known points determine both the slope and the anchor; when the anchor is where the line cuts the y-axis at (0, c) the equation shortens to y = m x + c.
concepts.key_idea: All the standard forms are rearrangements of one idea -- slope times horizontal travel equals vertical travel.

concepts.title: Intercept Form of a Line
concepts.definition: If a line cuts the x-axis at a and the y-axis at b (both non-zero), its equation can be written with those two intercepts as x/a + y/b = 1; the triangle formed with the axes then has legs of lengths a and b.
concepts.key_idea: Intercept form trades slope information for the two crossing points on the axes.

concepts.title: Distance of a Point from a Line
concepts.definition: The shortest gap between a point (x0, y0) and the line A x + B y + C = 0 is found by substituting the point into the left side, taking the absolute value, and dividing by the square root of A squared plus B squared.
concepts.formula: dist = abs(a_coef * x0 + b_coef * y0 + c_coef) / sqrt(a_coef ** 2 + b_coef ** 2)
concepts.key_idea: Substitute, take absolute value, normalise by the length of the normal vector -- three moves that give perpendicular distance.

solution_steps.explain: Dividing the absolute displacement by sqrt(a_coef**2 + b_coef**2) converts it to true perpendicular distance.

concepts.title: Distance Between Two Parallel Lines
concepts.definition: For parallel lines written with the same A, B coefficients, the gap between them is the absolute difference of their constant terms divided by the square root of A squared plus B squared; the shared denominator is the length of the common normal direction.
concepts.key_idea: Slide along the common normal: only the constants differ, so their difference scaled by the normal length is the gap.
